toc.title: How to strengthen your vagal brake
The vagal brake and daily life

blocks.p: The "vagal brake" is the influence of the safety state on the heart. If the ventral pathways are active, they keep the heartbeat calmer and reduce flight/fight activation. Without them, heart rate increases significantly, activating the flight/fight state.

The vagal brake is not a physical thing, like a biological flap or gateway. It's the influence of the safety state. If the safety state is inactive, then the vagal brake is off. If the safety state is active, then the vagal brake is on. The safety state keeps the defensive states in check. Mammals don't live in defensive states like flight/fight and shutdown only. We have a third state, the safety state, that repurposes defensive states for prosocial behaviors.

Repurposing defense results in play, stillness, and intimacy. Humans can "...rapidly engage and disengage with objects and other individuals and to promote self-soothing behaviors and calm behavioral states." The vagal brake allows for a middle ground where we can quickly and efficiently access mobility and immobility while remaining connected to others, ourselves, and the present moment. Without the vagal brake, we would constantly be immobile or mobile but in defense: running, fighting, shutting down, or freezing.

blocks.h: How to strengthen your vagal brake

blocks.p: You strengthen your vagal brake like you would anything else: by exercising it! That means utilizing your safety state. Practice feeling safe.
"But I don't know how to feel safe, that's the problem!"

Right. But still, this is the starting point. Think of it this way: if you want to lift 200 lbs, you need to start somewhere, right? You won't lift 200 lbs before you lift 100. And you won't lift 100 before you lift 50. But you'll reach your goal of 200 by starting with what you can and then building from there. You don't need to meet the entire goal the first time. Practice with what you're capable of, then repeat, challenging your capacity.

Your goal may be to eventually feel love, patience, kindness, and confidence. That's great. But can you meet those goals right now? Probably not. But can you inch your way in that direction? Yes. Right now, you feel enough curiosity to read this. You feel enough motivation to read and reflect. So, you already have some level of safety in your system. That's what you start with, then challenge what you can handle and repeat.
"Cool, Justin, but how?" you ask with impatience.

If you consciously exist in the present moment, that's probably a really good indicator that you're utilizing your ventral vagal pathways. If that's true, then that means you're now exercising that system and building the strength of your vagal brake. It gets more complicated, but that's the basic idea.

blocks.why: Being in the present moment exercises the vagal brake. This practice is a few minutes of that.

blocks.p: Let's get a little more complicated...

"Pendulation" refers to the mindful and conscious exercise of pendulating, going back and forth, from defensive activation to safety. If one can anchor in safety, they may then become curious and open to their internal experiences, even stuck defensive ones.

The process of titration comes along with the process of pendulation. Titration is feeling into and releasing the stuck defensive energy a bit at a time. The key is to do so in small doses, not all at once. And to do so mindfully while anchored in safety. Titration allows small bits of stuck defense to discharge, allowing more capacity for feelings of safety.

blocks.h: The vagal brake and daily life

blocks.p: A strong enough vagal brake leads to pendulation and titration. These are both fantastic skills you can use in your trauma recovery journey. The vagal brake also brings benefits to your daily life.

Life becomes more manageable and less threatening. Your heartbeat is calmer, with less potential to be triggered by benign or even negative things. You will still neurocept people and events that are truly dangerous as danger, shifting to flight/fight as needed based on context. From the safety state, you're better at recognizing safety and danger on a biological level.

Work, school, and relationship stresses are less triggering in daily life. Parents who would otherwise yell at their child have more patience. The jerk at work is no longer as upsetting. Listening to friends and partners comes from empathy and understanding. We don't experience these little to big daily assaults on our autonomic nervous system as dangerous. Instead, they are manageable pieces of everyday life.

q: "Because the nucleus ambiguus is an integral component of the medullary system generating the respiratory rhythm (Richter & Spyer, 1990), the output of the vagal fibers terminating on the heart are characterized by a respiratory rhythm of increasing and decreasing tone (Porges, 1995). The functional consequence of this rhythmic modulation of nucleus ambiguus vagal tone to the sinoatrial node is to produce the respiratory oscillations in the heart rate pattern known as respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA). Thus, the quantification of the amplitude of RSA provides an index of the dynamically changing status of the vagal brake." (Porges et al)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W., Doussard-Roosevelt, J. A., Portales, A. L., & Greenspan, S. I. (1996). Infant regulation of the vagal “brake” predicts child behavior problems: A psychobiological model of social behavior. Developmental Psychobiology, 29(8), 697–712.

blocks.p: My translation: Scientists can measure safety state activation through RSA. (Pretty cool.)

q: "The theory functionally states that if you are confronted with a challenge, based on evolution, the most recent part of your nervous system will attempt to negotiate safety by using the face and vocalizations. If that doesn't work, the social engagement system will be withdrawn including the vagal inhibition on the heart (i.e., vagal brake), which would increase heart rate to promote mobilization in anticipation of defending with fight/flight behaviors. If that doesn't work, then you're going to ramp up the sympathetic nervous system for fight/flight. If you can't escape or fight, then you may reflexively shut down." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W. (2011). The Pocket Guide to the Polyvagal Theory: The Transformative Power of Feeling Safe. W. W. Norton & Company.

blocks.p: My translation: In danger, you use your safety state, then flight/fight, then shutdown. It's the reverse of how the states evolved within us. We use the newest system first: safety.

q: "Mammals have a unique vagal system that includes myelinated fibers that regulate heart rate. The mammalian vagus functions as an active vagal brake in which rapid inhibition and disinhibition of the vagal tone to the heart can change cardiac output to promote immediate engagement and disengagement with objects and individuals... [D]uring states of mobilization, characterized by classic "fight-flight" behaviors and sympathetic excitation, both the vagal brake and the behavioral components of the social engagement system are not easily accessible." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W. (1998). Love: An emergent property of the mammalian autonomic nervous system. In The Polyvagal Theory: Neurophysiological Foundations of Emotions, Attachment, Communication, and Self-regulation (2011). W. W. Norton & Company.

blocks.p: My translation: Mammals have a safety state which acts as a brake for defensive activation. When the brake is off, flight/fight takes over.
